stem: What is the aim of gene therapy?

options.content: To add a working allele to a patient's cells
To remove every faulty allele from the body
To replace a patient's blood with donor blood
To produce a hormone in bacteria for later injection

explanation: Gene therapy inserts a working allele so that the cells make the functional protein.

stem: Which statement describes somatic gene therapy?

options.content: Body cells are modified, so the change is not inherited
Gametes are modified, so all descendants carry the change
An embryo's cells are modified at the eight-cell stage
A protein is injected instead of a gene
options.rationale: That is enzyme or protein replacement.

explanation: Somatic therapy affects only the treated person's body cells.

stem: Which vector inserts the therapeutic gene into the host cell's chromosomes?

options.content: A liposome
options.rationale: Liposomes deliver DNA without integrating it.

options.content: An adenovirus
A bacterial plasmid
options.rationale: Plasmids are not used to integrate genes in human therapy.

options.content: A retrovirus
options.rationale: Correct: reverse transcriptase makes DNA, which integrates.

explanation: Retroviral (and lentiviral) vectors integrate DNA into host chromosomes.

stem: Why are liposomes sometimes chosen as vectors instead of viruses?

options.content: They insert the gene into chromosomes more reliably
They deliver DNA into far more cells than viruses do
They make the effect permanent and inherited
They are less likely to trigger an immune response

explanation: Liposomes contain no viral proteins, so they provoke less immune response, but they are less efficient.
hints: What does the immune system recognise on a virus?

stem: Why is the retina a good target for gene therapy of an inherited eye disease?

options.content: Its cells divide rapidly, so the gene spreads to the whole body
It is small, easy to inject and shielded from immunity
Its cells have no DNA, so the new allele faces no competition
options.rationale: Retinal cells have nuclei with DNA.

options.content: It can be removed, treated and replaced in the eye
options.rationale: The vector is injected in vivo.

explanation: A small, accessible, immune-privileged tissue of non-dividing cells keeps expressing the gene.
hints: Think about access, size and immunity.

stem: Why is gene therapy more straightforward for recessive conditions than for dominant ones?

options.content: Recessive alleles are removed automatically when a new allele is added
One added working allele can supply the missing protein
Dominant alleles cannot be transcribed in somatic cells
Recessive conditions affect only the gametes

explanation: In a recessive condition, the problem is a missing functional protein; adding a working allele supplies it. A dominant allele's harmful product would still be made.
hints: What would the dominant faulty allele still do?

stem: In a gene therapy trial, some patients developed leukaemia several years later. Which explanation is most likely?

options.content: The new allele was not expressed, so the original disease returned
The liposomes fused with each other inside the bone marrow
The vector inserted beside and activated a cell-division gene
options.rationale: Correct: insertional activation of an oncogene.

options.content: The patients' immune systems destroyed all the treated cells
options.rationale: This would end the treatment, not cause cancer.

explanation: Random integration by retroviral vectors can switch on proto-oncogenes, leading to uncontrolled division.

stem: Which is a reason commonly given for not permitting germ-line gene therapy in humans?

options.content: It cannot affect any cell of the resulting child
Its effects would be too short-lived to matter
It only works for dominant conditions
options.rationale: This is not the reason given.

options.content: Descendants cannot consent to the change

explanation: Changes would pass to all descendants, who cannot consent; errors would also be inherited, and enhancement is a concern.
hints: Who else would carry the change?

stem: A person treated by somatic gene therapy cannot pass the faulty allele to their children.
explanation: False. Their gametes are unchanged, so they can still pass on the faulty allele.

stem: Viruses used as vectors in gene therapy are modified so that they cannot replicate and cause disease.
explanation: True. Genes for replication and disease are removed.

stem: Match each problem of gene therapy with its cause.

right.content: Vector inserts beside a gene that controls cell division
Too few target cells take up the vector
Treated cells die and are replaced by untreated ones
The body recognises viral vector proteins as foreign

explanation: Each problem has a biological cause.

stem: Choose the correct words.

payload.template: In ADA-deficient SCID, toxic products kill developing {{blank:a}}. In gene therapy, the patient's bone marrow {{blank:b}} cells are removed, given the normal allele and returned, which is an {{blank:c}} method.

explanation: Lymphocytes; stem cells; ex vivo.

stem: Name the enzyme whose deficiency causes one form of severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID).
explanation: **Adenosine deaminase (ADA)**.

stem: Of $4.0 \times 10^{8}$ stem cells treated with a lentiviral vector, $1.1 \times 10^{8}$ expressed the new allele. Calculate the percentage of cells expressing the allele.
explanation: $\dfrac{1.1 \times 10^{8}}{4.0 \times 10^{8}} \times 100 = 27.5\%$. Dividing the wrong way round gives over 100%, which is impossible.
workedSolution: 1. $\dfrac{1.1 \times 10^{8}}{4.0 \times 10^{8}} \times 100 = 27.5\%$. Dividing the wrong way round gives over 100%, which is impossible.
hints: Divide the number expressing by the number treated.

stem: After gene therapy for an inherited eye disease, a patient could detect a test light at 18 positions on a screen, compared with 3 positions before treatment. Calculate the percentage increase.
explanation:
1. Increase $= 18 - 3 = 15$.
2. Percentage increase $= \dfrac{15}{3} \times 100 = 500\%$.
3. 600% is the after value as a percentage of the before value, not the increase.
workedSolution:
1. Increase $= 18 - 3 = 15$.
2. Percentage increase $= \dfrac{15}{3} \times 100 = 500\%$.
3. 600% is the after value as a percentage of the before value, not the increase.
hints: Divide the increase by the starting value.

stem: Outline how gene therapy can be used to treat SCID caused by ADA deficiency.

points.description: Normal ADA allele inserted into a (harmless) retroviral / lentiviral vector
Bone marrow stem cells removed from the patient
Cells infected with the vector in the laboratory; allele integrates into their chromosomes
Cells returned to the patient; they make ADA and produce lymphocytes that survive

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The normal ADA allele is inserted into a harmless retroviral or lentiviral vector. Bone marrow stem cells are removed from the patient and infected with the vector in the laboratory, so that the allele becomes integrated into their chromosomes. The cells are returned to the patient, where they make adenosine deaminase and give rise to lymphocytes that survive, restoring immune function.

explanation: Vector, ex vivo stem cells, return, expression.
hints: Which cells give rise to lymphocytes?

stem: Explain four problems that have limited the success of gene therapy.

points.description: Effects short-lived: treated cells die / non-integrated DNA is lost, so treatment must be repeated
Immune response against the viral vector or the new protein destroys treated cells / reduces repeat doses
Integrating vectors insert randomly and may activate an oncogene, causing cancer
Difficult to deliver to enough target cells / expensive

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Effects are often short-lived, because treated cells die and are replaced, or the added DNA is lost when cells divide, so treatment must be repeated. The immune system may recognise the viral vector or the new protein as foreign and destroy treated cells. Retroviral vectors insert at random and may activate an oncogene, causing cancer. It is also hard to deliver the gene to enough target cells.

explanation: One mark for each problem explained.

stem: Discuss whether germ-line gene therapy should be permitted in humans.

points.description: For: could permanently remove a serious inherited disease from a family / all cells corrected
Against: future generations cannot consent; errors or side effects would be inherited
Against: long-term effects unknown / could lead to enhancement (designer babies)
Views differ: some religious groups oppose altering the germ line; most countries currently do not allow it; a reasoned conclusion

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Supporters argue that germ-line therapy could remove a serious inherited condition permanently, since every cell of the child would carry the working allele and it would not be passed on. Opponents point out that future generations cannot consent, that any error would be inherited, that long-term effects are unknown, and that it could lead to enhancement of normal traits. Some religious groups oppose altering the human germ line. Because of these risks, most countries do not permit it at present.

explanation: Balanced discussion with a conclusion.

stem:
A child with ADA-deficient SCID received bone marrow stem cells modified with a lentiviral vector carrying the *ADA* allele. T lymphocyte counts (cells per mm³ of blood) were measured.

| Months after treatment | 0 | 3 | 6 | 9 | 12 | 15 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| T lymphocytes / cells per mm³ | 80 | 410 | 820 | 1150 | 1240 | 1260 |

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Calculate the percentage increase in T lymphocyte count between month 0 and month 12, to the nearest whole number.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Describe the change in T lymphocyte count.

points.description: Rises steeply from 80 to 1150 cells per mm³ in the first 9 months
Then levels off at about 1240-1260 cells per mm³

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The count rises steeply from 80 to 1150 cells per mm³ over the first nine months, then levels off at about 1240-1260 cells per mm³.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Explain why the count stays high rather than falling back, as in early trials that treated mature T cells.

points.description: Stem cells divide repeatedly / are long-lived
The integrated allele is copied into every daughter cell, so new lymphocytes keep being made with working ADA

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Stem cells keep dividing throughout life, and because the lentiviral vector integrated the allele into their chromosomes, it is copied into every daughter cell. New T lymphocytes with working ADA are therefore produced continuously.

parts.label: (d)
parts.stem: Suggest two things doctors would monitor in this child over the following years.

points.description: Signs of leukaemia / abnormal expansion of one clone of cells (insertion risk)
Immune function / infections / ADA activity / antibodies against the vector

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Doctors would watch for leukaemia or abnormal expansion of one cell clone, because the vector inserts into chromosomes, and they would monitor immune function, infections and ADA activity in the blood.

explanation: Stem cell therapy gives lasting expression; monitor insertion risks.

stem: Two vectors are being considered for gene therapy of a lung disease caused by a recessive allele: an adenovirus and liposomes.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Give one advantage and one disadvantage of using the adenovirus.

points.description: Advantage: enters cells efficiently / delivers the gene into the nucleus without inserting into chromosomes (lower cancer risk)
Disadvantage: may trigger an immune response / effect is temporary as lung cells are replaced

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The adenovirus enters cells efficiently and does not integrate into chromosomes, so the risk of activating an oncogene is low. However, it may trigger an immune response, and the effect is temporary as lung lining cells are replaced.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: Explain how liposomes deliver DNA into cells.

points.description: Liposomes are phospholipid bilayer spheres containing the DNA
They fuse with the cell surface membrane (phospholipids), releasing DNA into the cell

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Liposomes are small spheres of phospholipid bilayer containing the DNA. They fuse with the phospholipid bilayer of the cell surface membrane, releasing the DNA into the cytoplasm.

parts.label: (c)
parts.stem: Why might treatment with either vector need to be repeated?

options.content: The allele is destroyed by the mucus in the lungs within minutes
options.rationale: This is not the main reason.

options.content: The treated cells become germ cells
options.rationale: Somatic cells do not become gametes.

options.content: Lining cells are replaced by cells lacking the allele
The allele makes the faulty allele dominant
options.rationale: Adding an allele does not change dominance in this way.

parts.explanation: Epithelial cells are short-lived; replacement cells come from untreated stem cells.

explanation: Vectors differ in efficiency, immunity and integration.
hints: Do lung lining cells last for ever?
